Zhou and Erdogan (2019) presented a two-stage stochastic goal programming model for the firefighting resource allocation and resident evacuation problem. The model considers multiple wildfire spread scenarios. The problem is defined on a raster landscape with variable cell sizes. The cell sizes depend on the fire spread rate in the relevant scenario. The fire spread is modelled spatially where the cells in the fire spread direction are marked as high-risk cells. When a high-risk cell is protected by the resources, it will not burn. The majority of the models in the literature treats the suppression resources as identical and always available. In a few studies, the operational characteristics of suppression resources are incorporated into the models. Rodríguez-Veiga, Gómez-Costa, et al. (2018) developed a MILP model to allocate air resources to a set of firefronts by considering resting times and refuelling constraints. The main difference of their model from our model is that the wildfire spread is not considered. Shahparvari et al. (2021) proposed a MILP model for the coordination of aerial suppression resources. The model minimises the total completion time and total costs. This study differs from ours in that the wildfire spread is not incorporated into the model. Instead, the resource requirements of each period are prespecified. Rodríguez-Veiga, Ginzo-Villamayor, and Casas-Méndez (2018) considered the working shifts and resting times of fire brigades and aerial resources in their MILP model. As their model is a fire-line based model, it does not address the impact of suppression on fire spread and provide a detailed response plan for each resource. In contrast, our model incorporates both direct and indirect effects of suppression activities. Belval et al. (2019) developed a grid based model which addresses control line quality, connectivity of firefighter travel paths, and safety constraints in ground suppression activities. In this study, a firefighter team begins travelling from one of the predefined access points, and can travel to the adjacent cells. It is assumed that the teams cannot travel through a cell more than once. Our modelling approach does not require such an assumption. In our model, the ground resources can only access to the incident zone through forest roads. In Belval et al. (2019), the effect of firefighting is modelled by a control line which reduces the fire intensity. In our model, the direct and indirect effects of firefighting and firebreak construction activities are defined in more detail. Moreover, the safety distance is dynamically determined according to the fire intensity in Belval et al. (2019). In our case, we have defined safety distances for the resources by taking the wind direction into account. Consequently, the safe working zones are updated when the wind direction changes. Note that characteristics of the terrain, as the slope and the type of vegetation, can also be easily incorporated in our fire spread model. To the best of our knowledge, there is no model that considers the coordination of multiple types of resources with their operational characteristics such as safety distance, availability of access to the firefront, and response time delays. Moreover, the effect of suppression activities on wildfire spread is modelled simplistically - a protection of a cell or a delay in the earliest fire arrival time. In this regard, the contributions of our study to the related literature are as follows: • We consider different types of resources (firefighter teams, firebreak construction teams, and firefighting helicopters) and their operational characteristics. This allows for a refined suppression plan, given that the resources need to operate under different constraints and can achieve different outcomes in extinguishing and limiting the spread of the fire. • The objective function of our model includes the damage caused by razing the forest land in addition to the burnt areas in overall damage calculation. Our model allows for prioritising infrastructure and areas of natural interest. • Our model explicitly accounts for the availability of access to the firefront through road networks. Firefighter teams and firebreak construction teams can only reach parts of the forest that are covered by road networks, leaving only the possibility of aerial resources to protect the rest of the area. Fire spread pattern The simplest fire spread pattern is circular in which the fire spreads from the ignition point at an equal rate in all directions. In the presence of wind, the fire spreads at a higher rate in its direction. In this case, the fire spread pattern resembles an ellipsoid (Anderson et al., 1982; Green et al., 1983). The elliptical fire spread pattern is illustrated in Fig. 2. In Fig. 2, Zones (a), (b), and (c) are the areas burnt by head fire, flank fire and back fire, respectively. The intersection point of all three zones is the ignition point. In a few study, the elliptical fire spread pattern has been incorporated into grid based modelling approaches (Wei et al., 2011; Zhou & Erdogan, 2019). Wildfire suppression The wildfire suppression tactics that we consider are ground and aerial firefighting, and firebreak construction. We have informed about the implementation details of these tactics by the interviews conducted with Muğla Regional Directorate of Forestry, and developed a modelling approach on raster landscapes accordingly. The following subsections present the implementation of these tactics and the details of our modelling approach on raster landscapes. 3.2.1. Ground and aerial firefighting The Firefighting Teams (FTs) are responsible for the ground firefighting. An FT consists of a wildland fire engine, a water tanker, and five firefighters. The wildland fire engines use water and firefighting foams for fire suppression. The fire engines and water tankers must travel fully loaded. The water tanker can be refilled from natural water resources such as sea, rivers, and lakes, as well as artificial lakes. The fire engines can be replenished by the water tankers without leaving its location. The fire engines are 4 × 4 vehicles that are able to travel through the forest roads. They cannot leave the forest roads and the firefighters access the firefront by laying hoses into the forest. Therefore, the length of the hoses constrains the extinguishing range of an FT. The fire engines should be at a safety distance from the firefront. The safety distance depends on the current wind direction. The fire engines cannot be directly in front of the head fire. The safety distance from flank fire is larger than that from the back fire. Consider the wildfire case illustrated in Fig. 3(c). Firebreak construction Firebreaks are the lines that serve as a barrier to slow down the progress of wildfire. A firebreak cannot catch fire as it contains no fuel. However, a fire can spread beyond the firebreak if its spread rate is large enough. A firebreak is built by removing all fuel (i.e. razing with a bulldozer) from a part of the forest land and digging down to mineral soil. Therefore, the forest land, where a firebreak is built, is damaged. However, it is reasonable to bargain away a part of forest land for protecting larger, possibly more valuable forest areas, or dwellings from a wildfire. In Türkiye, bulldozers are used for firebreak construction. As bulldozers move slower than the fire engines, the response time for the Firebreak Construction Teams (FCTs) is longer than that of FTs. Due to the same reason, the safety distance of the FCTs from the firefront is larger than that of the FTs. Unlike the FTs, FCT’s can work in front of the head fire but their safety distance from the head fire is much larger than that from the flank fire. Note that the safety distances are altered in case of a wind direction change as they are defined according European Journal of Operational Research 316 (2024) 488–502 493 M.G. Avci et al. Fig. 6. One can observe that the firefighting on the right side has distorted the shape of the fire by forming a natural firebreak by extinguishing. In particular, most of the firebreak construction efforts are in earlier time periods to obtain a firebreak as soon as possible. The fire spread on the left side has been mostly stopped by this firebreak. As a result of the coordination of firebreak construction and firefighting, the wildfire has been suppressed more quickly, and the total damage of the wildfire is lower. 3.3. Computational analysis This section presents a computational study performed on a set of randomly generated WSP instances. The set contains three groups of instances, with the number of cells being 25 × 25 (small-size), 50 × 50 (medium-size), and 100 × 100 (large-size). The forest roads were designed to be evenly distributed both horizontally and vertically. For an instance with 𝑚 ×𝑛 cells, the number of horizontal and vertical forest roads are determined as ⌈𝑚∕10⌉ and ⌈𝑛∕10⌉, respectively. Of the cells not belonging to forest roads, 10% of them were randomly selected to be non-flammable. The forest road cells and non-flammable cells have no value in terms of the objective function. The value of each flammable cell is generated by first selecting a random number 𝑟 from the interval (0, 10] and then rounding it to the smallest integer that is greater than or equal to 𝑟. The penalty coefficient 𝜌 for razing a cell was set to 0.1. The head fire, flank fire, and back fire spread rates are assumed to be identical for each flammable cell and determined as 4, 2, and 1 cells per time unit, respectively. The fire ignition points were randomly selected from the flammable cells. For the small-size instances, a single ignition point was considered. For the medium-size and large-size instances, the number of ignition points are {1, 2} and {1, 2, 3}, respectively. For each instance, the length of the planning horizon is 10 and the wind direction is from north to south for each time period. Note that, as the sizes of our formulations depend on the planning horizon length, we conducted preliminary experiments to appropriately set it in terms of both fire suppression requirements and computational burden. The response delay is set to 2 time units for the FTs and FHs, and 3 for the FCTs. To specify the levels of resources which are assumed to be constant over time, we examined Wildfire Suppression Action Plan of Türkiye (Orman Genel Müdürlüğü, 2021). We have observed that the number of FTs is always more than the number of FCTs and the number of FHs is always the least among all. Based on this observation, the sets of values for the number of FTs, FCTs, and FHs were determined as {5, 6, 7}, {2, 3, 4}, and {1, 2}, respectively. As a result, we obtained 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 different resource configurations. We generated one instance for each combination. Consequently, the small-size, medium-size, and large-size data sets contain 18, 36, and 54 instances, respectively. For the instances with multiple ignition points, the resource levels were multiplied by the number of ignition points. This is in line with the real-life cases because when more than one fire occurs in a region, the suppression resources from neighbouring regions can be sent to the relevant region. The data is provided in the online supplement. The formulations were coded in C++ and solved using Gurobi 10.0 (Gurobi Optimization, 2022). The lazy callback routine of Gurobi has been utilised to add the feasibility cuts (27) dynamically. The computational experiments were conducted on a personal computer with 4.00 GHz Intel Core i5-760X processor and 32 GB RAM. In all executions, we imposed a computational time limit of 3600 s. The results of the computational experiments are presented in Tables 2– 4 and Fig. 9. The detailed computational results are presented in the online supplement. This is an expected outcome since our model is deterministic and we have a complete information on when and in which direction the wind turns. With this knowledge, the FTs and FHs attack to the west side of the firefront. When the wind direction changes from the north to the east, the west side of the firefront is already under control. The controlled cells in the west serve as a firebreak to dampen the head fire spreading from the east. The results of this analysis highlights the importance of accurate weather forecast in wildfire suppression. Although predicting the wind direction and speed at certainty is not possible due to the chaotic nature of the weather, advanced forecasting techniques can provide very precise estimates (Wang et al., 2021). In practice, the wildfire professionals take advantage of wind change forecasts in their decisions. In this regard, Nuraiman et al. The ground suppression resources access the firefront by travelling on forest roads. In addition, forest roads serve as an anchor point in ground firefighting and firebreak construction. Hence, there is a trade-off between the effectiveness of wildfire suppression and the value lost during the road construction. In this context, we have performed a computational experiment to analyse the effect of forest road network structure on the effectiveness of wildfire suppression by varying the level of resources available to suppress the wildfire. The ignition points are the same for both network structures. The combinations of resource levels are the same as in the generated WSP instances. We generated one instance for each ignition point and resource combination. As a result, 324 additional instances were generated to perform this analysis. Case study To demonstrate the applicability of our model, we present a case study of wildfire suppression in Yatağan district of Muğla province, Türkiye. Yatağan has a high wildfire risk due to its typical Mediterranean climate with hot and dry summers. Moreover, approximately 70% of Yatağan surface area is covered by Turkish pine (pinus brutia) which is susceptible to wildfire. Therefore, Yatağan forest is classified as a first-degree wildfire hazard zone in Türkiye. Yatağan Directorate of Forest District (DFD) is responsible for forest management and wildfire suppression in Yatağan. Currently, Yatağan DFD has six FTs, an FH with night vision goggles and two FCTs (Orman Genel Müdürlüğü, 2021). When a wildfire escapes from the initial attack, the neighbouring forest directorates act in coordination to suppress it. Therefore, Yatağan DFD can quickly be supported by resources of other directorates in case of a large wildfire. Moreover, Yatağan DFD has a right to commandeer the vehicles of nearby mining companies for firebreak construction during a wildfire. In the case study, we consider a 5.504 km × 4.936 km region from a forest map provided by Yatağan DFD. A satellite image of the considered region is given in Fig. 11(a). We rasterised the region into 183 × 164 cells each of which has 0.03 km × 0.03 km size. The forest map provided by Yatağan DFD includes detailed information about forest flora, geographical formations, forest roads, infrastructure, and populated zones. We consider different fire spread rates for the cells depending on their fuel type. By consulting the managers, we have specified the fire spread rates as in Table 5. The highest fire spread rate is associated with the closed canopy Turkish pine and mixed forests while the spread rate on agricultural and residential zones is the lowest. As the back fire spread rate on maquis shrubland, degraded forest, agricultural and residential zones is negligible, we assumed that back fire cannot spread on the cells with these fuel types. The cells related to streams, lakes, mining zones, forest roads, and highways are marked as nonflammable since they do not contain any fuel. Conclusion In this study, we have addressed a WSP in which multiple types of suppression resources are considered with their operational constraints and effects on wildfire spread. We propose a basic IP formulation and a reformulation with combinatorial Benders’ cuts for the problem. Our formulations cover the operational characteristics and limitations of specific types of suppression resources. Additionally, it encompasses the impact of the suppression on wildfire spread with an explicit definition of distinct effects of the resources. We have tested our formulations on a set of randomly generated instances. The results indicate the effectiveness of the reformulation in solving the WSP. Moreover, we have presented a case study for the application of the proposed reformulation to a wildfire case in Yatağan district of Muğla province in Türkiye. The results obtained for the case study reveal the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in solving complex real-life problems. Our research is informed by interviews conducted with Muğla Regional Directorate of Forestry in Türkiye. Hence, the operational capabilities and constraints of the resources are modelled based on the ground and aerial suppression tactics and available resources in Türkiye. However, the models can be generalised to cover the characteristics of other types of resources with small modifications. The possible future extensions of this study may include different suppression tactics such as back-burning or the usage of unmanned aerial and unmanned ground vehicles. Moreover, the proposed model can be extended with routing decisions to incorporate the travelling of resources from one cell to another. Apart from these, a procedure to identify a proper upper bound on the length of the planning horizon can considerably increase the efficiency of the algorithm. Furthermore, heuristic approaches may be developed to find high quality solutions in shorter computation times.
